# What is a median? A mean?

The **mean** is the sum of all observations divided by the number of observations. The **median** is the middle value when the observations are ordered.(1)


# What is a variance? A standard deviation?

The **variance** measures the dispersion of the data around the mean, while the **standard deviation** is the square root of the variance and is expressed in the same unit as the data.(1)


# What is a normal distribution?

A **normal distribution** is a symmetric, bell-shaped probability distribution in which most observations are close to the mean and fewer observations are found further away from it.(1)


# What is a statistical test?

A statistical test is a method used to determine whether the observed data provide enough evidence to reject a null hypothesis about a population.(1)


# When to use a statistical test?

A statistical test is used when we want to determine whether an observed difference or relationship is likely to reflect a real effect rather than random variation in the sample.(2)


# What is a parametric test? A non-parametric test?

A parametric test relies on assumptions about the distribution and parameters of the data, whereas a non parametric test makes fewer assumptions about the underlying distribution and often uses the ranks of the observations.(3)


# What are the assumptions of parametric tests?

Common assumptions include an appropriate measurement scale, independence of observations, approximate normality of the data or residuals, and, for some tests, similar variances between groups.(3)


# What are the assumptions of non-parametric tests?

Non-parametric tests generally require fewer distributional assumptions, but they still require assumptions such as independence of observations and an appropriate study design.(1)


# What is a p-value?

The p-value is the probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed, assuming that the null hypothesis is true.(1)


# What is the risk of error when using a statistical test?

A statistical test involves the risk of making an error: a Type I error occurs when a true null hypothesis is rejected, while a Type II error occurs when a false null hypothesis is not rejected.(1)


# What is the difference between a paired and an unpaired test?

A paired test compares related observations, such as measurements taken before and after treatment in the same individuals, whereas an unpaired test compares independent groups of individuals.(2)
